title: 6  Bivariate Viz
text:
6.1 Exercise 2
# Set up the plotting frame
# A histogram only maps one variable on the x-axis while a scatterplot shows two quantitative variables
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16))
# Add a layer of points for each county
# Take note of the geom: geom_point
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point()
# Change the shape of the points
# The shape of the points change
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point(shape = 4)
# YOU TRY: Modify the code to make the points "orange"
# NOTE: Try to anticipate if "color" or "fill" will be useful here. Then try both.
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point(color = "orange")
# Add a layer that represents each county by the state it's in
# Take note of the geom and the info it needs to run!
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr))

title: 6  Bivariate Viz
text:
6.5 Exercise 6

ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_point()







A scatterplot is not ideal for visualizing the relationship between a county’s 2020 Republican support and historical political trends because it compares two quantitative variables, while historical trends are categorical. This makes it difficult to see clear differences between historically Republican, Democratic, or swing states. A boxplot or violin plot would better illustrate how Republican support varies across these categories.

ggplot(education, aes(x = sat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, fill = "blue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of SAT Scores by State",
       x = "SAT Score",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
Part B The SAT score distribution is not normal; it appears bimodal or right-skewed, with scores ranging roughly from 850 to 1200. Most states cluster between 900 and 1100, but some have notably lower averages. This pattern is likely due to differences in SAT participation rates—states with low participation often have higher average scores since only strong students take the test. Additionally, state testing policies and education funding may contribute to these variations.

title: 7  Mulivariate Viz
text:
7.2 Exercise 2

ggplot(education, aes(x = expend, y = sat)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "SAT Scores vs Per Pupil Spending",
       x = "Per Pupil Spending ($1000s)",
       y = "SAT Score") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









ggplot(education, aes(x = salary, y = sat)) +
  geom_point(color = "green", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "SAT Scores vs Teacher Salary",
       x = "Teacher Salary ($1000s)",
       y = "SAT Score") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Part B The plots show little to no positive correlation between SAT scores and both spending and teacher salary, which is surprising. This is likely due to SAT participation rates—states with higher spending often have more students taking the test, including lower-performing ones, which lowers the average score.

title: 7  Mulivariate Viz
text:
7.4 Exercise 4

ggplot(education, aes(y = sat, x = salary, color = cut(expend, 3))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








If you change the 2 to a 3 it divides per pupil spending into three levels instead of just 2.
The plot shows that SAT scores are more strongly influenced by per pupil spending than teacher salaries. States with lower spending tend to have higher SAT scores, likely due to fewer test-takers, while higher spending states often have lower SAT scores because more students take the test. Teacher salary seems to have less impact on SAT scores in comparison.

Part A

ggplot(education, aes(x = fracCat)) + 
  geom_bar()







Part B the more students in a state that take the SAT, the lower the average scores tend to be. This is probaly related to self-selction

ggplot(education, aes(x = sat, fill = fracCat)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)







Part C When we control for the fraction of students that take the SAT, SAT scores increase with expenditure.

ggplot(education, aes(y = sat, x = expend, color = fracCat)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Part D Student participation tends to be lower among states with lower expenditures (which are likely also the states with higher ed institutions that haven’t historically required the SAT). Those same states tend to have higher SAT scores because of the self-selection of who participates.

# Construct a univariate plot of goals_scored (no wrangling necessary)
# This provides a visual summary of how the number of goals_scored varies from World Cup to World Cup
ggplot(world_cup, aes(x = goals_scored)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "white")

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.









# Let's follow up the plot with some more precise numerical summaries
# Calculate the min, median, and max number of goals_scored across all World Cups
# NOTE: Visually compare these numerical summaries to what you observed in the plot
world_cup |> 
  summarize(min(goals_scored), median(goals_scored), max(goals_scored))

1                70                  126               171



# Construct a bivariate plot of how the number of goals_scored in the World Cup has changed over the years
# No wrangling necessary
ggplot(world_cup, aes(x = year, y = goals_scored)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line()








# Our above summaries might be a bit misleading.
# The number of games played at the World Cup varies.
# Construct a bivariate plot of how the typical number of goals per game has changed over the years
per_game_data <- world_cup |> 
  mutate(goals_per_game = goals_scored / games)

ggplot(per_game_data, aes(x = year, y = goals_per_game)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line()
